questions.question: In a Feistel network, why can decryption use the same round function F as encryption?
options: Because XOR is invertible and the halves swap each round, so you can undo the round by reversing key order
Because F is always a bijection on the right half
Because the initial and final permutations cancel the need for decryption
Because DES uses the same subkey in all rounds
questions.explanation: A Feistel round is invertible even if F is not, as long as you can recompute F and XOR with it, using round keys in reverse.

questions.question: What is the block size of DES (and therefore also 3DES/TDEA)?
options: 64 bits
56 bits
128 bits
256 bits
questions.explanation: DES is a 64-bit block cipher; 3DES reuses the same 64-bit block primitive three times.

questions.question: Which expression matches the standard 3DES/TDEA forward (encryption) operation in EDE form?
questions.explanation: TDEA encryption is defined as encrypt with K1, decrypt with K2, then encrypt with K3 (EDE).

questions.question: DES keys are often written as 64 bits (8 bytes). Why is the effective key size only 56 bits?
options: Each byte includes a parity bit that is not used by the key schedule
DES discards 8 bits because the initial permutation removes them
DES uses only 56-bit plaintext blocks
DES compresses the key with a hash to 56 bits
questions.explanation: The key schedule drops one bit per byte (parity), leaving 56 effective key bits.

questions.question: Why is a 64-bit block size a practical security problem for long-lived encryptions (e.g., CBC/CTR with huge volumes)?
options: Because birthday collisions become likely after about 2^32 blocks under one key/IV context
Because it makes brute-forcing the key easier by a factor of 2^64
Because it forces you to use ECB mode
Because it prevents padding from working correctly
questions.explanation: With 64-bit blocks, the birthday bound is around 2^32 blocks; collisions leak structure and can enable practical attacks in some settings.

questions.question: If your DES implementation fails known-answer tests, which bug is most likely?
options: A permutation/table bit-ordering mistake (e.g., interpreting table positions from LSB instead of MSB)
Using too many rounds (more than 16)
Using little-endian integers instead of big-endian in hex parsing only
Forgetting to include the final swap of halves is never an issue
questions.explanation: DES is extremely sensitive to bit numbering and table application; off-by-one or MSB/LSB interpretation errors are common.

questions.question: Why didn’t “Double DES” (encrypting twice with two independent keys) give ~112-bit security in practice?
options: Meet-in-the-middle attacks reduce the work to roughly 2^57 time and 2^56 memory
Because parity bits reduce the key space to 56 bits total
Because S-boxes make two encryptions cancel out
Because DES decryption is identical to encryption
questions.explanation: Meet-in-the-middle allows matching intermediate values between the two encryptions, far cheaper than brute-forcing both keys.

questions.question: A TDEA key bundle with K1=K2=K3 effectively reduces to what?
options: Single DES
AES-128
A secure 3-key construction
A one-time pad
questions.explanation: EDE with identical keys collapses to single DES, which is why standards forbid all-three-equal key bundles.
